Le Canada est l’un des plus grands donat: Canada is one of the world's largest donors of international aid, notably for projects deemed “progressive and feminist,” which it funds around the globe. La Converse travelled to Lebanon, the seventh-largest recipient of Canadian funds, to analyze two development aid projects and examine their limits.
Comment envisager une réelle solidarité: How can we imagine real solidarity between the North and the South?
À une époque où les inégalités se creuse: At a time when inequalities are growing and anti-racism is gaining ground, it is important to reflect on ways of helping, including through art.
rue principale d’al Qalamoun, bordée de: The main street of al Qalamoun, lined with cafés and houses whose façades were repainted by the NGO Utopia, is heavily travelled. North Lebanon, 12/11/2022, Philippe Pernot
Le résultat est enchanteur. Une panoplie: The result is enchanting. A wealth of colours and a series of murals cover the entire downtown of Al-Qalamoun, a fishing village in northern Lebanon. From historic shops to newer cafés, they accompany walkers from the highway all the way to the seafront. You stroll along dreamy-eyed, relaxed and amazed.
Le projet « Al-Qalamoun en couleurs » co: The project “Al-Qalamoun in Colour” began in 2019, when Utopia, a Lebanese NGO, decided to carry out an art project in this small coastal town 75 km north of Beirut.
« On voulait profiter à la jeunesse, don: “We wanted to benefit young people, so we talked to the municipality, consulted the population, and it was the young people who chose to paint the walls rather than do activities,” explains Shafik Abdulrahman, one of the NGO's founders. A hashtag was created, the project got people talking, and tourism went up.
« On remercie l’ONG, le résultat est bea: “We thank the NGO, the result is beautiful. It had a big impact on the youngest,” Rim Kaddour tells us over the phone. The young woman is one of the 120 people who painted their town's walls, alongside fine arts students and a Palestinian artist.
Salma el-Hendi et sa famille discutent d: Salma el-Hendi and her family talk in their apartment, where one wall was repainted blue by Utopia but the others are run-down and eaten away by damp. Qalamoun, North Lebanon, Philippe Pernot
Mais une fois le projet terminé, les pro: But once the project was over, the structural problems resurfaced: the houses are just as dilapidated as before, the infrastructure is deteriorating, and the roads, full of potholes, are more and more dangerous to drive on.
« Tout conducteur passant par là détruir: “Any driver going through there would wreck their car because of the huge number of cracks and potholes. The situation is truly shameful,” says Marwan, Rim's father, who runs a candy shop. “We would have preferred interior renovations rather than exterior ones. It would have helped us more, especially psychologically,” says Salma el Hendi, a Palestinian resident of Qalamoun. She is surrounded by her neighbours and women from her family, and all of them say the NGO never asked them what they wanted.
« Nous avons dû supplier un des ouvriers: “We had to beg one of the workers to paint one of the walls inside our home,” she tells us in her small apartment, which does nothing to block out the winter cold. The place is damp, and mould covers the walls. “It smells bad, and sewage water from our neighbours seeps into our home. The houses here are old; if they were renovated, they would be magnificent, but there's no money,” she continues. These problems should be taken on by the city and the state.
« Nous souhaitons une intervention de la: “We want the municipality to step in to maintain the roads and infrastructure,” sums up Rim Kaddour.
Ce coup de peinture ne suffit pas à régl: This coat of paint is not enough to solve the systemic problems of the town and the country. At first glance, such art projects are positive and harm no one. But looking more closely, they contribute to the inaction of public authorities and are out of step with people's needs.
Le projet d’Utopia devient donc une méta: Utopia's project thus becomes a metaphor for Lebanon, where development aid masks misery and feeds the state's neglect.
Trois des cinq œuvres murales réalisées: Three of the five murals created by the French NGO Artivista in the marginalized neighbourhood of Bab el-Tebbaneh, by Aurélie Andres (France) and MJay (Lebanon), JoBer (France) and Abrash (Lebanon), respectively. The two murals not visible in the photo were created by Exist (Lebanon) and Zdey (France). Tripoli, North Lebanon. Photo: Philippe Pernot
Pour Utopia et son donateur, le projet a: For Utopia and its donor, the main goal of the project was to be seen and to generate tourism, rather than to thoroughly renovate housing. That intention takes priority in many NGO initiatives, according to Clothilde Facon, a researcher in political sociology at Université Sorbonne Paris Nord. “In general, this kind of project meets a need for visibility, which is crucial for donors,” explains Facon, who works specifically on NGOs operating in Lebanon. It was indeed the GIZ (Deutsche Gesellschaft für internationale Zusammenarbeit), the German state development agency, that directed the choice of project.
Les jeunes du village ont été consultés,: The village's young people were consulted, but only after the decision to go with an art project had been made. This reproduces a neocolonial logic, according to Clothilde Facon. “There is a power imbalance, and it is Westerners who impose their vision and their solutions on countries of the South,” she says. This approach, though at the forefront of development aid, is the same one Canada uses, among others. When NGOs from the Global North carry out a project in a country of the South, they involve local groups, but without giving them decision-making power.
Or, « la prise de décision est cruciale: Yet “decision-making is crucial in development,” Facon points out. Even when a call for projects goes out from a Northern NGO to the South, local organizations have to conform to Western expectations and self-censor to obtain funding, or because they have internalized Western methods, she says. Beyond marketing, there is also the image of the donor or the NGO's owner. “They want recognition, and that comes with the white saviour complex.
C’est une forme d’aide qui est liée à un: It is a form of aid that comes from an excellent intention, but that also serves to make people feel better,” continues Maïka Sondarjee, author of Perdre le Sud, décoloniser la solidarité internationale (2020), a book in which she deconstructs the development aid and humanitarian sector and offers solutions for helping better, that is, in a decolonial way.

L’artiste français JoBer en train de cré: French artist JoBer creates a mural in Bab el-Tebbaneh for the French NGO Artivista, depicting Phoenician figures. Tripoli, North Lebanon, Philippe Pernot
La population d’Al-Qalamoun n’est pas la: The people of Al-Qalamoun are not the only ones to experience the joys and frustrations of an art project. A few kilometres farther north, in Tripoli, Lebanon's second-largest city and also the poorest in the entire Mediterranean basin, a French association decided to “bring art” to one of the city's most marginalized neighbourhoods: Bab el-Tebbaneh. Grey, decrepit apartment blocks rise up, pockmarked with bullet holes, and garbage litters the streets. Only a few façades are covered in murals, which are masterful and colourful.
Artivista y a inauguré un projet de <em>: Artivista launched a street art project there on five façades renovated and repainted by Lebanese and French artists. The goal was to “pass on street art as a means of expression to young people, and joy to their hearts,” says founder Claire Prat-Marca. She says she fully involved the neighbourhood's residents and organizations and carried out renovations in two buildings to meet their needs. “The repainted wall faces the outside of the neighbourhood. People on the highway can see it and admire it, but not us,” retorts Sabah Ali Jawhar, a mother in her sixties who lives in one of the buildings involved.
Elle nous reçoit sur son balcon décrépit: She welcomes us onto her crumbling balcony, which looks vaguely onto a mural, and serves us coffee flavoured with cardamom. “We thank the NGO, it brings joy to our hearts, but we would have liked the work to be done on the inside, more on the neighbourhood side, or in our homes, which are run-down,” she says, adding that Artivista did not consult her before work began. Mould covers the walls of her apartment, which is plunged into darkness by a power outage. Since the crisis, the state provides no more than two hours of electricity a day at most, and running water has become a luxury. “Installing solar panels or water tanks would really have changed our daily lives,” says the mother.
Un graffiti représentant le projet “Qala: A graffiti piece representing the “Qalamoun in Colour” project by the NGO Utopia in the tunnel at the entrance to the village. North Lebanon, 12/11/2022, Philippe Pernot
L’artiste et doctorante à l’UQAM étudie: The artist and UQAM doctoral student studies the relationship between humanitarian work and Indigenous people. She conducted her master's research on artistic intervention and work teams in the humanitarian field. “Art can have different intentions and must be used with a receptive audience. We can ask, with these two projects [Artivista's in Tripoli and Utopia's in Al-Qalamoun], whether it was the right moment,” says the doctoral student, who points out that there is a difference between humanitarian aid and development aid.
L’humanitaire répond à des situations d’: Humanitarian aid responds to emergencies, whereas development aid targets persistent problems. “When there is an emergency, it's not the time to propose art,” explains Rajoelisolo-Debergue. And Lebanon is currently going through the worst economic crisis in the world since 1850: the currency has lost 90% of its value, 82% of the population lives below the poverty line, and two-thirds of Lebanese people skip a meal. “We want something that benefits us as human beings, not just a pretty view from the outside. We want nothing more than our basic rights: most of the children in the neighbourhood go to sleep without eating or drinking,” sighs Sabah Ali Jawhar. In this context, projects focused on food or basic infrastructure might have been more appropriate.
Une femme marche devant un dessin mural: A woman walks past a mural popular with young people on social media, in downtown Al Qalamoun. North Lebanon, 12/11/2022, Philippe Pernot
Pour autant, l’art peut réellement avoir: Still, art can genuinely have immediate effects on people's stress, mental health and resilience, says Rajoelisolo-Debergue.
« La pratique joue sur l’affect, sur la: “The practice plays on emotion and creativity, but also on the engagement of the population,” the researcher continues. She argues that artistic expression initiated by local communities “can be part of the solution and lead to decolonial forms of development aid.” For her, the most important thing remains adapting art projects to the real needs of residents. Maika Sondarjee agrees. In her view, North-South artistic exchanges must continue. “We need to bring Canadian artists to see what artists in other countries are doing, for example.
On peut apprendre beaucoup du Sud global: We can learn a lot from the Global South. But we have to stop sending young people with Québec sans frontières to ‘help’ people in countries of the South,” she says. “To help in a less colonial way, you have to work fully with a local organization and arrive on site with no preconceived idea of the project. That's the hardest part, because you have to accept not imposing graffiti if the population wants something else,” the researcher continues.
« Le travail d’une ONG du Nord dans un p: “The work of a Northern NGO in a country of the South is not necessarily a problem; it's how it's done that can be problematic,” explains the professor of international development. For Sondarjee, the big problem lies in the condescending and paternalistic side of international cooperation. She argues that, to avoid this trap, local movements and communities' own ways of doing things would need to be made more visible. Artivista seems to have picked up on this point, notably by involving a university and a school in anti-corruption workshops.
Cependant, Maïka Sondarjee précise qu’il: However, Maïka Sondarjee stresses that it is not enough “to include in order to be decolonial.” “You can try to be innovative, to do things differently, and that can be interesting if the initiative is local, but it often comes at the expense of people's real needs,” she explains.
Ces propos sont confirmés par des person: These remarks are borne out by people we met in Bab el-Tebbaneh. There, a need for justice and equality is rumbling. “Here, there is no justice, the government made us poor. In Beirut it's different, there's money, it looks like Italy from here,” says the mother, one of whose sons lives in a boarding school in the capital and another has been languishing in prison for five years without a trial.
Dans son visage souriant, seuls les yeux: In her smiling face, only her eyes and wrinkles hint at the hardship of life in the neighbourhood. Bab el-Tebbaneh has a reputation as a dangerous, violent area plagued by crime. For Ms. Jawhar, these are the consequences of poverty and of underdevelopment willed by the centralized state. “Most of the children here have no education or job, they are powerless, and when you have that kind of situation, violence results,” she sighs.
C’est précisément ces inégalités structu: These structural inequalities are precisely what NGOs do not help eliminate. “Humanitarian and development aid don't change the system,” says Clothilde Facon, a PhD candidate at Sorbonne Paris Nord. In her view, the very large number of NGOs, which exert a strong pull, among other things by offering above-average salaries, “diverts” toward development aid young people who would otherwise have gotten involved in activism, politics or civil society. This is the famous “NGO-ization” she studies in her research. “NGOs depoliticize what is happening in Lebanon. The situation is approached simply through a purely humanitarian lens,” she laments. The problem?
Cela tue la société civile. « Dès qu’il: It kills civil society. “As soon as there is a political or activist aim behind a project, it loses its funding and its visibility. This creates a dichotomy between overvalued humanitarian NGOs and civil society ones that lack resources,” she explains.
Soutenir plus d’organisations locales po: Supporting more local alternative political organizations would, for her, be an essential path toward real change. “The work of these Lebanese organizations is essential to reforming the political system, which is problematic,” the researcher stresses. And what if, in order to help, we stopped trying to help? For Maika Sondarjee, it would be a matter of promoting “radical solidarity” between allies. “We could see redistribution as an act of social justice,” she continues. Ceasing to see the Global South as a place where famine and humanitarian crises are concentrated would make it possible to see that the struggles being waged in Lebanon and elsewhere are often the same as in Canada, since they concern wages, women's rights, social rights, housing, racism and inequality.
